claims.claim: Groundwater is water stored in the open spaces within rocks and unconsolidated sediments below the land surface; the water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation.
In areas with topographic relief, the water table generally follows the land surface, comes closer to the surface in valleys, and intersects the surface where there are streams, lakes, or springs.

Porosity is the percentage of a material's volume that is open space; permeability is how easily water moves through interconnected openings, so a material can be highly porous yet nearly impermeable.

An aquifer is a water-bearing body of rock or sediment that stores and transmits enough water to supply wells and springs; an aquitard is a low-permeability layer. A confined aquifer between low-permeability layers can hold water under pressure, and a well tapping it can have water rise or flow to the surface without pumping (artesian conditions).

Groundwater moves slowly through connected pore spaces from higher to lower water-table elevation, commonly centimeters per year to centimeters per day, and in some permeable materials several meters per day; this contrasts with fast, channeled flow in surface rivers.
Fresh groundwater is about 0.7 percent of all of Earth's water and roughly 30 percent of Earth's fresh water (USGS estimate based on Gleick).

Aquifers are recharged by infiltration of precipitation; where pumping removes water faster than recharge, water tables drop, wells can go dry, and fine-grained aquifer sediments can compact so the land surface subsides.

In the United States, more than 17,000 square miles across 45 states have been affected by land subsidence, and more than 80 percent of identified subsidence has been caused by exploitation of underground water.

Groundwater can be contaminated by natural and human-induced sources; contaminants such as pesticides and fertilizers can migrate to the water table and move with groundwater flow, and contaminated groundwater is very difficult to clean up.

In karst regions, circulating groundwater dissolves soluble bedrock such as limestone, carbonate rock, and salt beds, creating caves and caverns, and sinkholes form when the land surface collapses into enlarged underground openings.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reported groundwater flow speeds differ between sources.
positions: USGS: in some permeable materials groundwater may move several meters in a day; in other places only a few centimeters in a century.

Open Textbook BC: velocities of several centimeters per day are possible in significantly permeable sediments with significant gradients; it is not uncommon for flow to be a few millimeters to a few centimeters per year.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The ranges overlap and both sources describe slow pore-space flow whose speed depends on permeability and gradient. The lesson presents the combined range: centimeters per year to centimeters per day, with meters per day possible in very permeable material.
